I hope to have a chance to come back to third country training, but I think that it is one of the most important forms of training CIDA can give because it does not deprive the student of his culture. It keeps him in the general area to which he is accustomed. He is living at all times with people with whom he can speak and communicate. He is learning things he can readily take back to his home land, but I received no response on that.
In Panama there is an institute of community co-operation operated by a Canadian priest, Father Steele. It had been operating for ten years without any assistance. CIDA was there and Padre Steele would ask me on more than one occasion whether there was any possibility of my persuading CIDA to get two or three students to this institute so that he could train them and send them back into the country from which they came to develop community ideas. All the courses were in Spanish; there were no problems of language. But do you think I could get anything from CIDA-again a matter of third country training? Not at all.
I think the most unfortunate experience I had with CIDA mismanagement is well recorded in some letters which are on file. I do not think I am breaking any trust in telling the story. I was refused permission as ambassador to Nicaragua to visit an area where there was the prospect of a port being built. I was told not to go there because it might indicate that Canada was much too interested in helping finance that port. I had other arrangements to visit Canadian communities in the area which I had to cancel.
Within two weeks of that refusal a junior officer from CIDA was sent to that area. He did not even bother to visit the port but approved the participation of Canada in the building of it, went home, and did not even tell the ambassador from Canada to Nicaragua that he had done so. I found out months later that this had been done because I went to see some of the officials in the Nicaraguan government, and they said that Canada had been so helpful to them. I asked them to tell me about it because I did not know that. A junior officer in CIDA had come and negotiated and concluded an agreement concerning a port which the ambassador was not allowed to even look at!
These are the things we want to bring to the fore. These are problems which arise in all countries. There was another one in Costa Rica. There was a course in universi-

ty administration which had been started and stumbled somewhat. When the negotiators came down to conclude the agreement, I had been given no briefing. I almost was not invited to the meeting, but I arranged to be there, and I was expected to expound on the benefits of this particular course. I did not even know there was a plan.
The lack of co-ordination between the Department of External Affairs and CIDA is appalling, and it is time the minister knew it.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but the time allotted to him has expired.
I would like to-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan).

Madam Speaker, I think most of us can agree that the Canadian International Development Agency needs to be more responsive to the requests for less secrecy, despite the plea of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson), and more open about its policies, programs and goals. I think an admirable suggestion has been made by my colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), that a separate ministry be established for overseas development.
In the debate of November 15 on the world food crisis we mentioned that Canada, as with the United States, had not achieved its promised goal of supplying the least developed countries with even 1 per cent of its GNP. This is very disturbing to many of us, but we do not want to see Canada fulfilling that goal for its own sake but rather as a means of being helpful in the short and long run development of these countries. In this connection we want to ask: Is it true, as some commentators have recently suggested, that CIDA is rushing to spend $117 million within the next three months in an effort to impress Treasury Board officials?
We are all acquainted with the notion that if we do not spend what we have been allocated, they, the institution granting the money-in this case the Treasury Board- might reduce the allotment for the next year. I repeat, can this be true? In view of the fact that CIDA has now had some six years of experience, and given the incredible short run need for food aid and the long-term need for development of the 32 most needy countries, surely this cannot be true. Surely it is a false accusation that the chief emphasis of CIDA is placed on producing figures to support the impression that Canada is in the vanguard of nation providing development assistance.
Surely, Madam Speaker, it is false to say that in CIDA, a major criterion of success is not how well you spend the money but how much of the money you have been allocated in the budget you spend, and that you spend your allocated money, come hell or high water.
We know that at a time of world-wide inflation and structural changes in international economies, and of

February 20, 1975

uncertainties in international monetary relations, CIDA faces great difficulties in adjusting and, indeed, changing its programs, projects and objectives in the foreign aid and development field.
We should not be surprised that such a complex job should carry with it internal administrative strain and personal unrest. These are all additional reasons, Madam Speaker, for an open and frank re-appraisal of CIDA by parliament. The government should not be afraid to show CIDA's warts, because such a re-appraisal will be a condition for a renewed international aid and development effort on our part as we enter the second half of the 1970s. A renewed, re-invigorated CIDA will allow us to meet the new and severe challenges of the 1980s in the international development field. According to most experts these new challenges will be much more severe than those we face in the 1970s. We will be facing a situation in which not only aid and trade problems vis-a-vis the least developed countries will still be with us; we shall also face a situation in which we, in the very well-off countries, must balance our attempts to overcome our wasteful habits by conserving energy, food and raw materials, with commitments by the poorer countries to change some of the worst features of their agricultural, demographic and environmental practices.
In the longer run, requirements for development in the least developed countries will mean that CIDA and similar agencies in other countries will have to play a greater role in giving such countries access to our markets at stable and remunerative prices. Likewise, they will need much greater access to our technology, management skills and investment capital. But the major goal for them has to be to learn by doing, because imitating and borrowing would satisfy neither their material needs nor their higher needs for greater control of their economic and cultural destinies. Hopefully on this matter CIDA officials will impress on them all that they should not follow our own historical development path as a model.
There are still and will be in the short run very pressing needs for customary food and other forms of aid. I might add that I disagree slightly with the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) on this issue, although I agree with almost everything he said this evening. There is a tendency today to dismiss this aid as being a failure, without attempting any serious analysis. Nevertheless, I still suggest that such aid is still very necessary for the development of these poor countries.
We mentioned in the November 15 debate that if hundreds of thousands of people are not to die during the next decade, mechanisms must be developed in order to plan food supplies on a world basis. The United States and Canada must lead the way. The money costs will be enormous and will have to be shared. But, Madam Speaker, that is the challenge we dare not fail to accept. At times it seems to be most forbidding; yet only if it is met will we have time to make realties of our longer run hopes for population control and new agricultural developments in poorer countries.
Some think it is already too late, that mass starvation cannot be avoided. That may be so, but it is necessary, in any event, to try. After World War I, in a disrupted

Europe, John Maynard Keynes wrote poignant words which are well worth remembering. He said:
Men will not always die quietly. For starvation, which brings to some lethargy and a helpless despair, drives other temperaments to the nervous instability of hysteria ... These in their distress may overturn the remnants of organization, and submerge civilization itself in their attempts to satisfy desperately the overwhelming needs of the individual. This is the danger against which all our resources and courage and idealism must now co-operate.
As we are discussing the immediate plight of some of the poorest countries, will the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) say what CIDA's present role is in the Sahalian zone of West Africa, where there are some 25 million hungry people? Will we supply fertilizer to Bangladesh during the coming year or, more generally, are there such commitments in the form of loans or grants for fertilizer for that desparate country?
I urge the government, Madam Speaker, to make CIDA's internal and external problems better known to members of parliament who represent the Canadian people, so that we can help in making CIDA a better institution, one of which we can be even more proud in future.

Madam Chairman, when I heard that the opposition had decided to devote one of the alloted days to the discussion of the problems of international cooperation and the role of Canada in that field, on the one hand, I was happy because it seemed to me that it was the very occasion to make Canadians aware of the importance of those questions, which, as we know, draw more and more attention. We become more aware of the global aspect of the world community. We realize that during the last twelve months, the whole world has changed so that a problem existing on a continent which could have seemed very far from us a few years ago, has implications in the daily life of those we represent here as members of Parliament. On one hand, I was very glad, but on the other hand, I felt some apprehension because the opposition wanted to devote one of the days they are entitled to the discussion of a question of their choice, and I thought: they must certainly have terrific arguments; they are surely going to bring astounding accusations which will put our government on the spot.
We have been debating this matter for a few hours. In some cases, the debate was more or less acrimonious. Still we have been discussing this matter for some hours. I listened carefully to all the speakers, to the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) and to the others.
Who?

The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe. He is entitled to that title. I respect him.
I listened to him carefully and, finally, I realize that as in all the debates we have in this House, the opposition unfortunately did not play the important part it should play in a democracy. The role of the opposition is to give positive criticism. The opposition may occasionally make interesting suggestions which enable the government to run the nation's business more efficiently in a country like Canada.
February 20, 1975

I listened to them carefully and I must say that in some cases some interesting ideas have been expressed. I will come back to them. But it seems to me that, in most cases, we could call it a torrent of words in a desert of ideas. Unfortunately that is what we have heard since the beginning of the debate.
A suggestion which has some merit and is worth looping into is that CIDA should be put under the direct control of cabinet minister. Of course, in view of the growing importance of international cooperation and since it is a matter of increasing concern across Canada, this suggestion has certainly some merit. It should, however, be said that while in the past war was the extension of the foreign policy of countries-unfortunately this still rings true for some countries-but for us Canadians it is international cooperation which constitutes the extension of our foreign policy. Accordingly, I find it reasonable, normal and natural that the international cooperation programs launched by the Canadian government be the responsibility of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen).
In fact, I believe that this has enormous advantages even from a functional viewpoint. I have had the opportunity to live more or less with these matters, and I know that there is some kind of osmosis between the department and CIDA, which means that as concerns personnel, for instance, external affairs employees are often transferred to CIDA and vice versa.
While I am on this subject, I would like to take a few moments to speak of this alleged very great turnover within CIDA personnel. I have here some figures which show that, in fact, the rate of personnel turnover at CIDA is lower than the average rate throughout the entire Canadian public service. For instance, the figures for people who left CIDA show that in 1974-75, 3 per cent of the executives and 4.9 per cent of the support employees left the agency.
On the other hand, people left CIDA for other departments. I would like to say something about this, but I will simply give the figures, which are 3.5 per cent for the executives and 3.1 per cent of the personnel who brings the required support to the operation of the Canadian International Development Agency.
In my opinion, it is impossible to make a judgment on personnel turnover in an organization like CIDA in the same way as in another government department, quite simply because CIDA employees work in extremely different and extremely difficult conditions. There is much travel, the employees must live in foreign countries, there are adaptation problems, and in my opinion it is normal that some of the employees must eventually give up their jobs.
Madam Speaker, I would like to say a word about the accusations concerning the allegedly secretive operation of the Canadian International Development Agency. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) pointed out this afternoon, it seems to me the opposition has every opportunity, every chance to ask all their relevant questions, first when the estimates of that agency are considered, second when the public accounts committee meets.

On the other hand, it is common knowledge that the president of CIDA, Mr. Gerin-Lajoie, never hesitates to meet with journalists. Never does he shy from talking to people in the academic field or specialists in international matters. He is remarkably available. I would specifically like to pay tribute to Mr. Paul Gerin-Lajoie.
I remember the contribution that man made at the beginning of the silent revolution in Quebec, specially with respect to the reform of the education system in Quebec. If today we have a better educated youth in Quebec, a youth that can make an increasingly substantial contribution to the direction of this country, the direction of Quebec, I think we must pay tribute to Mr. Paul Gerin-Lajoie.
Madam speaker, I would not want the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) to feel he has to rise on a question of privilege. I think he did inadvertently. I also think there are unpleasant things to say but they must nevertheless be said. I think perhaps unintentionally he made himself an accomplice of that swarm of journalists, of those pontiffs of the press who in recent months, in recent weeks, had the gall to attack, not CIDA as such, because there was absolutely nothing one can find to prove that CIDA does not have a sound management under the leadership of Mr. Paul Gerin-Lajoie.
I think there is some disappointment in certain quarters to see francophones come to Ottawa and really carry out their responsibilities and not just be fronts.
There was also the case of the president of Air Canada who was criticized and viciously attacked. Why? Because a Francophone came forward, accepted a responsibility in a federal government agency and decided to assume his responsibilities seriously.
Shame!
There you are. Madam Speaker-
The ministers are not saying a word. They are still.
Because the hon. member for Montmorency is trusted.

Madam Speaker, I expressed some surprise a while ago when I spoke of prejudice. We are going to talk about that. I was surprised that some offence was taken at the fact that through the Canadian International Development Agency the Canadian government should have established ties with the Cuban government with regard to international co-operation.
Let no one make me say that I agree with the political regime in Cuba. Still, to my mind, the foreign policy of a country like Canada should strive towards drawing countries closer, uniting them, all the more so in the case of Cuba, since Canada has always insisted on maintaining trade relations with that country and since the loan granted to the Cuban government will affect the economic development in Canada, in that Canadian companies will give work to Canadian workers who will benefit from contracts representing the amount loaned to the Cuban government.

February 20,1975

Madam Speaker, perhaps we should make efforts individually to see not so much each one of the trees but the whole forest. When an agency has a budget of more than $700 million, that will reach $900 million next year, it is obvious that some programs must inevitably have weaknesses and deficiencies. Those who lead that agency are men, only men-
This is Women's Year!

Man in the most general meaning of the term! Perhaps we should try to see in what context the International Development Agency must operate. There have been changes in the last 10 or 25 years. Today's world is even already different from what it was a mere twelve months ago. Changes have occurred in the world situation. The countries with which we have established international co-operation programs have seen their needs evolve, the Canadian people have expectations that vary with each group, they have expectations that are different according to the various groups they are made of. The government may also have various objectives.
The subject of changes in the world situation can be tackled from a more concrete point of view with examples such as the changes brought about by the oil crisis. We see for instance countries such as Algeria, Nigeria, Indonesia which, from underdeveloped countries that they were before oil got as important as it is now, have become less dependent upon international aid.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired.

Madam Speaker, all Canadians are interested in the present debate. All across the country, people ask themselves if their tax money is spent rationally by the government and by CIDA. If there is an area where the taxpayers' money is spent in an unacceptable way, it is in the sector of foreign assistance.
That is why, Madam Speaker, I want to take part in this important debate which gives" us the opportunity to show to the Canadian people the unbelievable waste that is made of the taxpayers' money in the area of foreign assistance.
We, of the Social Credit Party, are not opposed to the principle of assisting countries that need help. We believe that Canadians have a responsibility towards underdeveloped and underprivileged countries. For that reason, we advocate technical and material assistance to enable those countries to become self-sufficient as soon as possible. That is also why we, of the Social Credit, object to foreign aid programs which maintain those countries in their state of underdevelopment.
A careful study of the activities of CIDA shows that this agency, in addition to swallowing millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money, systematically supports assistance programs that are as costly as they are useless. We also see that the person who is mainly responsible for that situation is the present president of CIDA, Paul Gerin-Lajoie, former Quebec education minister and personal friend of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).

It would be impossible to enumerate in a whole book the examples of colossal blunders and indecent waste that must be put to CIDA's credit. Madam Speaker, I shall simply give a few particularly striking examples.
In 1974, Canada granted $5 million to Brazil through CIDA. I believe that country is rich enough to have its own foreign aid program. Indeed, it suggested Canada pay the $5 million to the Brazalian foreign aid program. Finally, Canada paid a total $84 million to Nigeria, Indonesia and Algeria, all oil rich countries. Cuba, in turn, the democratic "paradise", received a $10 million loan, without interest, for 50 years, at the moment sugar was bringing fantastic revenues.
Madam Speaker, in spite of Canadian experience and expertise in agricultural matters, and a desire on the part of underdeveloped countries to tap that experience, only 3 per cent of Canadian foreign aid, or $23 million on a total $349 million, involved technical assistance. This means a mere 3 per cent of Canadian assistance was spent on helping underdeveloped countries help themselves and become truly independent.
On humanitarian grounds, CIDA paid significant amounts to various terrorist groups that spent that money on bombs and arms needed to kill those who opposed revolutionary wars. For example, $100,000 went to terrorists in South Africa, to help them in their destructive work.
CIDA also supplied a number of countries with totally useless products. Magnificent fountains were built in front of buildings erected by CIDA in a certain African country. The only problem is in that country, water is so scarce it is more expensive than oil. It is not wasted in fountains. CIDA also spent thousands of dollars to buy outboard motors to be used on dugout canoes in Senegal.
No more examples are needed to convince any person of good will that something is wrong in CIDA. The fact is known that in two years, more than 300 CIDA employees resigned. This excessive figure shows even civil servants find CIDA is not performing normally.
If CIDA does not work properly, it is first and foremost because it is not controlled by the elected representatives of the people. Mr. Gerin-Lajoie did not have to be elected. Neither does he have to answer questions in the House of Commons as any minister does. Yet, only two other ministers have higher budgets to administer, namely the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson).
Madam Speaker, Canadians would perhaps have less cause to complain about CIDA if, instead of being headed by a friend of the Prime Minister, that agency was headed by a minister of the Crown answerable to this House.
I repeat what I said earlier: We, Social Crediters, are in favour of foreign aid. On the other hand, we refuse to accept the wasteful practices of CIDA under its president, Mr. Gerin-Lajoie.	.
We believe CIDA should be made into a department. Thus, we could, every day call to account the minister responsible for foreign aid. That is what we demand, Madam Speaker. If the government is logical, they will surely follow the suggestions made today by the opposition.
February 20, 1975

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the time remaining I hope to be able to put forward a few points.
I congratulate the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) on his motion. First of all I should like to say that it is indicative of the state of affairs in our government today, and in the various departments, that we should choose this topic for an opposition day motion. It is appalling that we should have to debate in this House whether or not parliament has the right to examine the actions of the chief of a government agency. There has never been a time in the history of our country and of our parliament when this has been a matter of discussion.
Of course we have a right to question the activities of any and all government departments and agencies, and we have the right, indeed we have the duty, to question the actions and the conduct of any and all chiefs of departments and agencies. When you consider the fact that we are actually debating whether we have the right and the duty to examine the expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayers' money, then I have to ask whether or not someone has reversed the natural order of things.
Have we really reached the point where a chief of a department has the right to refuse to divulge information on his activities to the Canadian parliament? If that is what the president of CIDA thinks, and if that is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) thinks, then all I can say is that those two gentlemen have a few things to learn about the Canadian system of parliamentary government.
This day of debate on the activities of the Canadian International Development Agency has not come a bit too soon. At a time when parliament is trying to find out why CIDA has to rush to get rid of almost $200 million before the end of the current fiscal year, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) has announced that the CIDA giveaway budget is to be increased by $200 million in the coming fiscal year. Newspaper columnist Richard Gwynn asked the question, in his column of January 11 in the Journal: "Is CIDA a sick joke?" I think that we have the responsibility to determine whether or not CIDA is a sick joke before we approve such a massive increase in its budget. There are just too many indications that that is exactly what CIDA is, and there are indications that it is due to the actions of the boss of CIDA.
Our examination of CIDA must be extremely thorough, and it must have two primary objectives. We should find out exactly what is being done with the hundreds of millions of dollars that CIDA is giving away each year, and we should determine whether or not that money is accomplishing anything worth while. After all, this is tax money, money that has been grubbed from the Canadian taxpayers, and they have a right to know where it is being spent and whether or not they are getting full value.

Our second objective should be to determine the wisdom of keeping Paul Gerin-Lajoie, the former Liberal bagman, in the post of president of CIDA. Gerin-Lajoie has been running the agency with a free hand, making decisions that should be made by parliament and refusing to divulge even the most basic information about his activities; and the Prime Minister backs him in this.
Thanks to our press we have a picture of Mr. Gerin-Lajoie that makes him look more like an oriental potentate than a Canadian civil servant. He has little or no communication with anyone in CIDA outside his immediate associates in the upper echelons, and it has been said that some of the long time employees of the agency do not even know what their boss looks like. When he travels he has a larger entourage than a cabinet minister, and he seems to be able to travel wherever he likes, whenever he likes. There seem to be no checks whatever on his movements or of the money he spends on his travels.
His decision making powers appear to extend to every aspect of the agency's operations, and I commend my colleague, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds), for bringing to light still another aspect of his dictatorial handling of the agency. The hon. member revealed that CIDA's Latin American section has been designated unilingual French, meaning that the working language of the section is French. The hon. member charged that this policy makes it impossible for businesses in his constituency in British Columbia to deal with the agency, as those business people do not speak French. It is time for us to take a serious look at government policies that have made second class citizens of the majority of Canadians, those of our citizens who speak only English. I do not think our people are going continue to take that nonsense much longer, especially with this agency CIDA.
I support the demands that have been made for a complete and full inquiry into the activities of CIDA and of its chief, and that inquiry should proceed without further delay. In the meantime Mr. Gerin-Lajoie should be removed from the top position in the agency and for the time being, at least, the deputy chief of the agency should be placed in charge of both policy and administration. That move alone would, I am sure, go a long way towards re-establishing credibility, efficiency and sanity to Canada's foreign aid program.
May I call it ten o'clock, Madam Speaker?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-ENFORCEMENT OF MAINTENANCE ORDERS ISSUED BY FAMILY COURTS- GOVERNMENT ACTION
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-ENFORCEMENT OF MAINTENANCE ORDERS ISSUED BY FAMILY COURTS- GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is the second time within a year that I have spoken on this subject, the enforcement of maintenance orders issued by family courts. In light of the fact that 75 per cent of all family maintenance orders made by Canadian family courts against deserting husbands are defaulted, and in light of the fact that these defaults cost Canadian taxpayers $365 million annually, this means that between January 1973 and today these defaults have cost Canadian taxpayers almost $1 billion.
As things now stand, a court order to a man for maintaining financially the family he has abandoned is often worth no more than the paper on which it is written. While the divorce law is federal, the laws that govern other aspects of marital break-up, maintenance, child support and property rights continue to vary as provincial responsibilities under the BNA Act. These responsibilities, though, are seldom enforced by the provincial courts; they leave that job to the deserted mother.
The federal government must act through whatever means possible to ensure that the job of tracking down deserting fathers is not left to deserted mothers. Presently a deserted mother not only has to track down her spouse but also has to keep returning to court for new maintenance orders if he defaults. As well, she has to hire a lawyer if he refuses to comply.
The Law Reform Commission has recommended that all matters of family law should be gathered together under one court. As the commission points out, it makes sense that the judge who grants a divorce should also deal with the division of marital property, child custody, access to the child by the parent who does not have custody, and the welfare and maintenance of the child. However, as was mentioned, the constitution presents a barrier for it splits responsibility for these matters between the federal and provincial governments and, therefore, the same case is handled by different judges in different courts. It seems obvious that the commission's recommendations should be adopted. I am hopeful that the federal-provincial discussions concerning the commission's recommendations will be a starting point for these much needed changes.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Marceau) answered me last March 25 and stated:
I note that my colleague has seen the conclusions of the Law Reform Commission working paper. I think we agree that the matter should be studied immediately, promptly and efficiently.
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
I hope that is what the government has been doing in the past 11 months. The parliamentary secretary went on to state:
The proposal advanced in the study paper, if endorsed by the Law Reform Commission, is one which might profitably be explored through the medium of the Conference of Uniformity Commissioners on Legislation in Canada which meets annually to examine ways and means of achieving uniformity in laws throughout the various jurisdictions.
I hope the hon. member can report on this conference tonight. He then went on to state:
I can assure my hon. friend that this matter interests me personally, as well as the department which I am representing tonight because I admit that it is time to truly deal with these problems unrestricted by jurisdictions which are necessary, but must not have priority over the population and the serious and important problems that my hon. friend has described and that I promise to refer to the minister. I also promise to give them particular attention myself.
What we need to rectify this problem is a federal wives' and children's maintenance act. I hope the parliamentary secretary can give a report tonight on the action that has been taken by the government, and indicate when proper government legislation will be introduced to rectify this serious problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilles Marceau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-ENFORCEMENT OF MAINTENANCE ORDERS ISSUED BY FAMILY COURTS- GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the matter of uniformly enforced legislation dealing with the reciprocity of enforcement of maintenance orders has been studied on several occasions by the conference of commissioners for a uniform legislation in Canada, since renamed the Conference for a uniform legislation in Canada.
The commissioners agreed to the last draft of that legislation in 1973. The matter of compulsory maintenance between husband and wife and between parents and children was on the order of the day of the 1974 Assembly. It was then decided to review that matter into greater detail during the 1975 meeting which will be held in Halifax, from August 18th to 22nd; the commissioners for British Columbia will then report progress on that matter.
The British Columbia Royal Commission on family law and children's protection is presently preparing reports and a bill dealing with alimonies and some other matters relating to family law. British Columbia also initiated in the Richmond-Surrey-Delta area a pilot project to test several recommendations dealing with that branch of law. The results of that double series of studies should enable the British Columbia commissioners to submit to the 1975 assembly proposals backed by practical experimentation of new solutions to family law problems.
Whatever the outcome of the studies, the enforcement of alimony and maintenance orders still remains a serious problem. Uniformly enforced legislation would certainly make the enforcement of those maintenance orders easier in the case of spouses who flee from one province to another but the main problem comes from those who, without stepping out of the courts' jurisdiction, deliberately omit payments. The beneficiary of the alimony engages into extremely costly procedures in order to try and have the order enforced himself or herself, and the spouse in default of alimony can frequently evade his or her responsibilities.

speechtext:
The Law Commission of Canada says on page 54 of its working paper No. 1 entitled Family Court:
The Commission believes that, with its complementary services, a family court could and should play a more active part in the implementation of the orders it issues. Some measures could be quickly adopted in the Canadian provinces and territories without imposing too heavy a burden on the judicial and legal mechanisms or on existing welfare services. These measures would comprise the establishment of enforcement services within the family court.
The measures referred to by the Commission could be implemented by each province separately, without having to wait for the passing of standardization legislation. Some provinces, such as British Columbia, already mentioned, and Ontario have moved in this direction.
A pilot project on the automatic enforcement of maintenance orders, put into force during two years by the Peel family court, became in August 1973 a permanent program that was extended theoretically to Ontario as a whole except that, given the shortage of staff and overflowing dockets, it has not been possible yet to put it into force in some areas of that province. In any event, the rule is that once the order is issued and registered in the office of the clerk of the court, the family court is responsible for its implementation.
As for the federal action, it took shape through correspondence addressed by the Minister of Justice to the attorneys general of all provinces, expressing his wish to cooperate with their governments in the reform of family courts. In this connection, the Department of Justice considers granting subsidies to pilot project in that field. Several provinces have shown a desire to participate in this kind of common undertaking with the federal government.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-INQUIRY WHETHER CANADA NEGOTIATING WITH BRAZIL IN PURCHASE OF ARMOURED CARS
NATIONAL DEFENCE-INQUIRY WHETHER CANADA NEGOTIATING WITH BRAZIL IN PURCHASE OF ARMOURED CARS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise tonight because the other day I asked two questions about Brazilian armoured cars which were not really answered. Hansard of February 11 records at page 3106 the following exchange between the minister and myself:

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-INQUIRY WHETHER CANADA NEGOTIATING WITH BRAZIL IN PURCHASE OF ARMOURED CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a seven-day old question for the Minister of National Defence. In light of the fact that a Brazilian-produced armoured car is now being tested at Camp Wainwright, can the minister now tell the House whether Canada has entered into negotiations with Brazil for these cars, and whether the cars are to be used for riot control or replacement for the Centurion, the Ferret or our armoured personnel carriers?
Adjournment Motion

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-INQUIRY WHETHER CANADA NEGOTIATING WITH BRAZIL IN PURCHASE OF ARMOURED CARS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is correct that we are testing armoured cars at Wainwright. One of them is from Brazil. There are other cars from Sweden and the United States. We have not made any decision, and we certainly have not entered into any negotiations with Brazil.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-INQUIRY WHETHER CANADA NEGOTIATING WITH BRAZIL IN PURCHASE OF ARMOURED CARS
speechtext: I understood the other car was from Switzerland, not Sweden; but I will let that go. Have the negotiations reached the state where the minister has consulted his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to determine if that minister may have reservations about a $200 million arms deal between Canada and Brazil?

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-INQUIRY WHETHER CANADA NEGOTIATING WITH BRAZIL IN PURCHASE OF ARMOURED CARS
speechtext:
I have already indicated to the hon. member that we have not entered negotiations for any arms purchase from Brazil.
So in sum I asked two questions. One was: what are they going to do with these vehicles, what are they to replace? The other was: have we any reservations about entering into negotiations with Brazil?
Of these three vehicles that are at present being tested in Camp Wainwright, one if from the United States, the Commando, which is basically an armoured personnel carrier although it can be converted to a reconnaissance vehicle or an armoured car. It weighs in the order of 15 tons, and is a most unlikely replacement for the Ferret. It is produced by the Cadillac Gage company of Detroit, Michigan. It may be of some consolation to Canadians to realize that we now have three Cadillac armoured cars in Canada, one at Camp Wainwright and two at 24 Sussex Drive.
One of the other cars that is considered in this competition is from Switzerland and is known as the Puma. The company, known as Mowag, has a Puma and a Tornado. The two cars weigh 16 tons each.
The information on the car from Brazil is rather difficult to obtain and most of it is contained in a copy of Latin America of October 18, 1974. It describes the two vehicles being made by Brazil, the EE-9 Cascavel, a wheeled reconnaissance vehicle, and the EE-11 Urutu, which comes in two forms-either an amphibious troop carrier for 14 men, or an armoured car. I think that from the description of these vehicles it is difficult to see how they can fill any of the known needs that we have in the Canadian armed forces, where the desperate need is for a reconnaissance vehicle to replace the Ferret, or for a tank to replace the Centurion.
If it is to replace the Centurion, Canada will end up with the world's thinnest-skinned tank. If it is to replace the Ferret we are going to end up with one of the heaviest imaginable armoured personnel carriers with a very indifferent cross country performance, being wheeled instead of tracked. I merely asked the minister the question the other day to try to obtain an answer because military men are puzzled when three vehicles, which are not anything like the top priority for replacement in our armed forces, are brought here for testing. One could easily fall into a state of conjecture and imagine that it is as a riot control vehicle, which is the main purpose to which these are put in the South American countries, according to Latin America.
The question of whether we should or should not buy it from Brazil is of interest to Canadians. Brazil is not a democracy as we know democracies. Brazil is not an ally of ours. The United States is certainly an ally, and there

February 20, 1975
Adjournment Motion
are other countries such a Great Britain producing very serviceable armoured cars and tanks.
I return to the main questions: what are we doing with these vehicles, what are they to replace, what is their use if we do buy them, and are we to assume that there is no preference to be given to the other nations in NATO?
I hope that the parliamentary secretary will be able to answer these questions because I am asking him for information, not to embarrass the department or the minister. I think there is quite an expression of interest in defence in Canada, and this needless and pointless secrecy only serves to confuse what may be a reasonable replacement program. I am sure that the Canadian people are now prepared to accept the fact that we do need replacements desperately, and particularly for our armoured vehicles.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leonard Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-INQUIRY WHETHER CANADA NEGOTIATING WITH BRAZIL IN PURCHASE OF ARMOURED CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as part of its re-equipment program the Department of National Defence has a requirement for an armoured wheeled personnel carrier, commonly known as an armoured car. This type of vehicle is being manufactured in a number of countries, including Brazil, France, Switzerland, Germany and the United States.
During the past summer, a technical procurement team from the Department of National Defence and the Department of Supply and Services examined ten different types of vehicles available on the international market. These government representatives visited the U.S.A., Brazil, France, Germany and Switzerland to examine at first hand vehicles being developed or in production.
Companies which had armoured cars which met the basic requirements of the Department of National Defence were asked to submit technical and financial proposals. Six proposals were received.
Following an intensive assessment by the government team, which considered such factors as technical performance, potential industrial stimulation and program price, three vehicles were selected which met the basic criteria. These are the Commando from the U.S.A., the Piranha from Switzerland and the Urutu from Brazil.
The technical assessment in progress last summer for an armoured wheeled vehicle was the normal preliminary step in examination of equipment needs which the Department of National Defence carries out. Models of all three vehicles are now undergoing winter trials at Camp Wain-wright, Alberta, to determine their performance under cold weather conditions. These trials commenced earlier in February and will not be completed until the latter part of' March of this year. The trials themselves are being conducted by soldiers from the Calgary based No. 1 Combat group under the supervision of factory representatives and specialists from National Defence headquarters.
Following completion of these trials and further detailed studies concerning technical performance, potential industrial stimulation and price, recommendation will be made to the government by the Department of National Defence seeking approval to begin negotiations to purchase the vehicle.

subtopic: AIR CANADA-ATTEMPTED DENIAL OF RIGHT OF MEMBER TO APPEAR BEFORE LABOUR BOARD-REFUSAL TO PAY EMPLOYEES APPEARING AS WITNESSES
AIR CANADA-ATTEMPTED DENIAL OF RIGHT OF MEMBER TO APPEAR BEFORE LABOUR BOARD-REFUSAL TO PAY EMPLOYEES APPEARING AS WITNESSES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, what I intend to discuss now relates to the incident in Montreal on December 4 before the Labour Relations Board when an Air Canada representative made representations to that board asking it, in effect, to rule that citizens appearing before the board should not contact their member of parliament, or members of parliament or ministers concerning matters which were before the board.
I think every member of the House readily agrees that that kind of request was ridiculous. Apparently Air Canada indicated to the minister that it had not authorized its representative to make that kind of representation. What is important about this instance is that it reflects the kind of attitude adopted by the labour relations division of Air Canada in the Montreal region; presumably this attitude exists outside the Montreal region as well. Nevertheless it reflects the attitude of Air Canada management to labour relations in general, and to its employees in particular.
This episode, so far as I am concerned, began in the latter part of 1973, when I was informed by several people working for Air Canada, who are constituents of mine, that the Air Canada labour relations division at Dorval was contributing to a serious deterioration in labour-management relations by the handling of the case of Mr. M. J. Morrison, chief shop steward at the power plant shop. Mr. Morrison was forced to work overtime on Dominion Day, 1973, even though it is a statutory holiday and is, by act of parliament, a public holiday. He had also been required to work on St. Jean Baptiste day, 1973, because Air Canada decided that that day would also be a normal working day.
After working five hours on Dominion Day, 1973, from 7.30 a.m. to 12.30 p.m., Mr. M. J. Morrison went home tired, leaving work three hours early. Mr. Morrison was 58 years old at the time and had worked 13 days without a break, and he was tired. But he was also angered by the callousness of Air Canada in misusing the power it has under the collective agreement to call in employees for essential work on holidays. It so happened that the so-called essential work that Mr. Morrison was called in to do could easily have been left until the next day. The call in for work on Dominion Day was purely and simply a show of power exercise by the company officials responsible. In any event, Mr. Morrison was suspended by Air Canada for five days, with a loss of pay privileges and a letter on his file, for being three hours absent without permission.
On January 15, 1974, I wrote to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) giving him the details of the incident and informing him of what I regard as an unsatisfactory labour relations situation at the Air Canada power plant at Dorval.

In that letter I wrote to the minister, I advised him that Air Canada was annoyed that Mr. Morrison had said in the past that the company had not observed public holidays and had asked its workers to put in too much overtime. According to Mr. Morrison's report on overtime, the company wanted the mechanics to exceed the overtime agreed
February 20, 1975

upon, namely 104 hours every three months. I was told that some employees worked from 160 to 180 hours overtime over a three-month period. Mr. Morrison also told about some defective parts of the company's equipment to the federal security agents.
As you can see, according to the above-mentioned events, Mr. Morrison did not precisely win the company's sympathy before this incident and one can easily conclude that the events previous to the incident influenced in some way Air Canada's decision to penalize Mr. Morrison because of his three-hour absence on the 1st of July. [English]
After some exchange of correspondence with Mr. Morrison, I wrote further letters to the Minister of Transport and to Mr. D. W. Benson, assistant to the president of Air Canada, on July 3, 1974. During the period from January to July, 1974, Mr. Morrison had also contacted the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) and had written letters himself directly to the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro).
The hearing of the Labour Relations Board was scheduled for September 23, 1974, and subpoenas were sent to a number of Air Canada employees to attend. The day of the hearing, it was cancelled because of the illness of one of the Board members, I believe the chairman, and Air Canada again demonstrated a reprehensible attitude toward its employees when, in spite of its internal regulations requiring that employees acting as court witnesses be carried on the payroll with pay, Air Canada refused to pay the employees who had appeared on behalf of Mr. Morrison.
I again wrote to the Minister of Transport on October 15 pointing out to him that Air Canada's refusal to pay the witnesses contradicted its own regulations and confirmed to me that Air Canada was deliberately and systematically trying to embarrass and punish Mr. Morrison and anyone having to do with his case. I pointed out that this continuing attitude was poisoning labour relations not only at the Air Canada power plant shop, but elsewhere in the Air Canada Dorval organization.
At the December 4 hearing, Air Canada again refused to pay the witnesses, even though they were subpoenaed by Mr. Morrison and, under company regulations, it was obliged to pay them their salaries.
I ask the parliamentary secretary who is here representing the minister tonight, to deliver strong urgings to Air Canada to rectify this miserable, miserly attitude toward its employees-

subtopic: AIR CANADA-ATTEMPTED DENIAL OF RIGHT OF MEMBER TO APPEAR BEFORE LABOUR BOARD-REFUSAL TO PAY EMPLOYEES APPEARING AS WITNESSES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first I wish to draw to your attention the fact that at page 3218 of Hansard for February 14, the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) stated:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question of privilege concerning a position taken by Air Canada-
I wish to emphasize the words "Air Canada". In a question directed to the minister this afternoon, the hon. member said "It relates to the incident in Montreal on December 4, when an Air Canada representative-". I emphasize the word representative. This evening, the hon. member again referred to the Air Canada representative.
This afternoon, in response to the hon. member's question, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) said, and I quote:

Mr. Speaker, the information I got from Air Canada is that this corporation has never instructed its legal adviser to hold that stance before the Canada Labour Relations Board. Therefore, that stance has been a purely personal one, and Air Canada dissociates itself completely from what has been said.
That is the answer given by the minister.

I think that even using only the part of the Air Canada counsel statement, as reported in Hansard on February 14, page 3218, it is obvious that the legal counsel was speaking on his own behalf. In fact the statement attributed to the Air Canada legal counsel was made after the union had withdrawn its complaint. It is my understanding that the union has re-filed the complaint and the board is now dealing with it. I do not think I should comment on the specific case.
However, the hon. member for Laprairie this afternoon, in his supplementary question to the Minister of Transport stated that Air Canada was in violation of its own regulations requiring payment of witness fees, requiring payments for its employees as witnesses and refusing to pay employees who appeared that day as witnesses on behalf of Mr. Morrison.
I believe it is the contention of Air Canada that the company regulations do not provide for indemnification by the company of the employee witnesses. Employees are granted time off with pay for jury duty, coroner's inquests or court duty. However, the circumstances in this case do not fall into any of the above categories.
